question.problem: $5%$ of electric bulbs are defective at manufacture. If six bulbs are randomly tested, with each one being replaced before the next is chosen, what is the probability that at least two are defective? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of defective tested bulbs. 

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=6$ tested bulbs

- the probability of choosing a defective bulb is $p=5%=0.05$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(6,0.05).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x})(0.05)^{x}(1-0.05)^{6-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x})(0.05)^{x}(0.95)^{6-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that at least two bulbs are defective. This corresponds to $P(X\ge 2).$

However, computing

$$
P(X\ge 2)=P(X=2)+P(X=3)+…+P(X=6)
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2) & =1-P(X<2) \\  & =1-[P(X=0)+P(X=1)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{0})(0.05)^{0}(0.95)^{6-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{1})(0.05)^{1}(0.95)^{6-1}] \\  & =1-[1(0.05)^{0}(0.95)^{6}+6(0.05)^{1}(0.95)^{5}] \\  & =1-0.967\,226 \\  & ≈0.033\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
